\chapter{Comieron --- One Ending, Two Families}
\label{ch:comieron}
\hlchaptermodality{201}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can put -er and -ir verbs into the plural past with one set of endings.}

I can put -er and -ir verbs into the plural past with one set of endings.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[comieron]{comieron}

\label{lesson:ES-C55-comieron}



\begin{quote}
In the past singular, how many ending sets do \emph{-er} and \emph{-ir} verbs need between them? (\textbf{One} — \emph{comí} and \emph{viví} take the same endings.)

The plural keeps that bargain.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: one ending, two families}]
\begin{quote}
\emph{\textbf{comieron}} · \emph{\textbf{vivieron}} — they ate · they lived
\end{quote}

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{} & \textbf{present} & \textbf{past} \\
\midrule
\emph{comer} & \textbf{comen} & \textbf{comieron} \\
\emph{vivir} & \textbf{viven} & \textbf{vivieron} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

The past ending is \textbf{-ieron} for both families, exactly as \emph{-í} served both in the singular. And \emph{we} follows the same shape:

\begin{quote}
\emph{comimos} · \emph{vivimos}
\end{quote}

Now the interesting part, and it is not the one you would guess.

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{} & \textbf{present} & \textbf{past} \\
\midrule
\emph{hablar} & \emph{hablamos} & \emph{hablamos} — \textbf{the same} \\
\emph{comer} & \emph{comemos} & \emph{comimos} — \textbf{different} \\
\emph{vivir} & \emph{vivimos} & \emph{vivimos} — \textbf{the same} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\textbf{Two families out of three collapse.} \emph{Vivimos} is \emph{we live} and \emph{we lived}, exactly as \emph{hablamos} is both. Only \emph{\textbf{-er}} keeps the two apart — and only because its past borrowed \emph{-imos} from the \emph{-ir} family and so moved away from its own present \emph{-emos}.

You met \emph{comemos} and \emph{vivimos} together as the first place \emph{-er} and \emph{-ir} stop agreeing. This is the second place, and it goes the other way.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{comieron · vivieron}
  \item \emph{comemos · comimos} — and \emph{vivimos}, which is both
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
The past \emph{they} ending for \emph{-er} and \emph{-ir}? (\textbf{-ieron}, for both.)

Which families lose the present-past distinction in the \emph{we} form? (\emph{\textbf{-ar}} \textbf{and} \emph{\textbf{-ir}} — only \emph{-er} keeps it.)
\end{tcolorbox}
